title: How this guide fits together
one_liner: Nine lifecycle stages, eight observed failure patterns, and six kinds of record joined by a graph drawn only from cited edges, with a pathfinder that ranks and never recommends.
why_here: A recruiter at a customer-governed small firm arrives with a symptom, an opening that will not fill or a person who is leaving, and the guide is built to narrow from that symptom to the constraints, rules and levers the evidence connects to it; knowing the parts makes the narrowing legible.

further_reading.title: Revisiting meta-analytic estimates of validity in personnel selection: Addressing systematic overcorrection for restriction of range
Surveying the forest: A meta-analysis, moderator investigation, and future-oriented discussion of the antecedents of voluntary employee turnover
32 CFR § 117.10, Determination of eligibility for access to classified information (National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual rule)

body_before:
## What it is

The spine of the guide is nine lifecycle stages in a fixed order: `plan`, `attract`, `select`, `offer`, `clear-start`, `onboard`, `develop`, `retain` and `handover`. Each stage record says what the stage is, which [failure patterns](#term:failure-pattern) surface there, which [gates](#term:gate-record) bind it and, in a field called `decided_by`, who controls the outcome. At the clear-start stage the government decides eligibility and its timing [119](#cite:119) [126](#cite:126). At the offer stage the contract sets the ceiling, since a [time-and-materials](#term:time-and-materials-contract) rate already contains the wage, the [indirect costs](#term:overhead-rate) and the profit and pays only for labor that meets the category's qualifications [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99). At the retain stage the person decides, on comparisons the firm only partly controls: wanting to leave and looking are the strongest predictors of quitting across 316 studies [178](#cite:178), and at one large retailer quits followed what higher-paid peers received more than the market [182](#cite:182).



Below the stages sit the records. The failure patterns are the [pathfinder](#term:pathfinder)'s first question: seven observed failure points from the author's original matrix, re-derived from the evidence, plus an eighth the plan sweep added, so the set reads `many-apply-few-qualify`, `withdraw-mid-process`, `few-plausible-candidates`, `pass-then-decline`, `accept-cannot-start`, `start-then-struggle`, `productive-employees-leave` and `customer-rejects`; each pattern points at [constraints](#term:constraint-record) with a cited reason. A constraint is what binds an opening, with its mechanism, the diagnostics that reveal it, who decides it and the strongest [evidence grade](#term:evidence-grade) among its sources. A [lever](#term:lever-record) is what the firm can do, carried with an evidence grade from the scope's vocabulary, the effect quoted as the study reported it with its population, and a field named `what_it_does_not_do` holding the trade-off or the limit. A gate is a rule, described in its own primer. An [enabler](#term:enabler-record) is a data source, program, reference, tool category or standard, recorded as its owner describes it, with no vendor recommended. An [indicator](#term:indicator-record) is a headline figure that travels with its reference period, publisher, publication date and, where one exists, a series identifier for the refresh.

The grade and the date are what make those records usable. The lever `l-structured-interview` carries the grade [meta-analysis](#term:meta-analysis) and the [operational validity](#term:operational-validity) .42 from the 2022 re-estimation, the highest of any single predictor [1](#cite:1). The [time-to-fill](#term:time-to-fill) indicator reads about 45 days, for 2025, from a survey of more than 2,300 SHRM members [43](#cite:43), and the [cost-per-hire](#term:cost-per-hire) indicator reads \$1,200 for a nonexecutive hire and \$10,625 for an executive one, for 2025, from 2,371 members [196](#cite:196).



The graph is drawn from one file and nothing else. Every [edge](#term:dependency-link) in the links file runs from a tail record to a head record with one of four relations: precondition, meaning the head cannot be addressed until the tail is; amplifies, meaning the tail makes the head worse; trade-off, meaning acting on the tail worsens the head; and enables, meaning acting on the tail makes the head easier. Each edge carries its own cited evidence and grade, and the step from evidence to edge is [marked synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker) wherever the cited works do not state it. In the first edge, an unvalidated screen is a precondition of a keyword screen that rejects qualified people, because years of experience carries an operational validity of .07 against .40 for [job knowledge](#term:job-knowledge-test) [1](#cite:1), and 88 percent of surveyed employers said qualified high-skilled candidates were rejected outright for not matching criteria exactly [44](#cite:44). The app's dependency walks follow these edges only.



The pathfinder asks four questions, the observed failure point, the stage if known, the role conditions and the state of work, and scores every record by a fixed rule: a pattern match counts 3, a stage match 2 and each matching condition 1; records scoring 0 are hidden, the page shows why each remaining record matched, nothing is recommended, only ranked, and the narrowed field passes to the graph as the highlighted set. The [decision record](#term:decision-record) is one record per opening, the pinned primary and secondary constraints, the chosen levers, an owner, a decision date and a measure, exported as Markdown or JSON and never leaving the browser.



The [hypothesis ledger](#term:hypothesis-ledger) records where the guide started. The author supplied a private staffing trade-off matrix of sixty rows in eight categories, with seven failure patterns, and called the rows best guesses that needed more rigor. Every row, category and pattern is carried as a hypothesis and never cited as fact, with a status from a fixed set, untested, supported, partly supported, contradicted, unstudied or reframed, and a cited evidence line once adjudicated. The ledger closed at version one with twenty entries supported, forty-three partly supported, eight reframed, four unstudied where nothing was found either way, and none left untested.
picture: The stage-map figure is a left-to-right band of nine boxes, with the eight failure patterns drawn as labels under the stage where each surfaces and in each box the deciders named in its `decided_by` field, so the clear-start box carries the government and the customer while the retain box carries the person. The ledger-outcomes figure beside it is a single stacked bar of the adjudicated entries, the supported segment, the larger partly-supported segment, the reframed categories and the unstudied rows.

## How this guide uses it



The scope record, the evidence-grade vocabulary, the list of marked syntheses and the ledger render on the methods page; the stage records render as the stage pages; constraints, levers, gates, enablers and indicators render in the node panel of the graph; the changes file renders as the changes page; and these primers render under concepts. The primer on reading a gate describes one record kind in depth, and the primer on reading an [effect size](#term:effect-size) explains how to read the validity and [correlation](#term:correlation-coefficient) figures the lever grades rest on.

title: Reading a gate, with its state overlay and its pending changes
one_liner: A gate record is a rule the firm did not write, carried with its governing text, the openings it applies to, the stages it binds, the state law laid over it, and the changes already dated but not yet in force.
why_here: A recruiter without an HR department meets these rules one opening at a time, and the same opening can sit under a federal contractor clause, a state statute and a change that takes effect next year; the record is built so that each of those is visible and separately sourced.

SB 26-189, Automated decision-making technology: initial fiscal note (Colorado Legislative Council Staff)
32 CFR § 117.10, Determination of eligibility for access to classified information (National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual rule)

body_before:
## What it is



A [gate](#term:gate-record) is the guide's record for a rule that binds an opening regardless of evidence: a statute, a regulation, a contract clause or an agency directive. Every gate carries the same fields. The `what` field states what the rule requires, each sentence cited to the governing text; `governing_text` names the statute or clause; `applies_when` gives the threshold or situation that brings the rule into play; `binds` lists the stages where it bites; `steps` are the actions the governing source itself describes; `pending_changes` holds dated entries with a status; and `conflicts` says where the sources disagree or where a fact rests on something weaker than a primary. The gate `nispom-eligibility-and-sponsorship` shows the shape: its governing text is [32 CFR 117](#term:nispom).10, it applies to any contractor in the National Industrial Security Program requesting eligibility for an employee, it binds four stages, and its steps follow the rule's own terms, including the start within 45 days of a grant for a hire investigated before employment [119](#cite:119).

A federal-contractor gate applies in every state, and the state record is laid over it. Each state record, one per state and the District of Columbia, carries nine overlays, pay-range posting, [salary-history bans](#term:salary-history-ban), [noncompetes](#term:noncompete-agreement), [stay-or-pay terms](#term:stay-or-pay-provision), AI in hiring, cannabis testing, fair chance, [credit checks](#term:credit-check-law) and [mini-WARN](#term:mini-warn-law) notice, each with a status, cited text, the federal gate it modifies and a flag saying whether a primary source sits behind it. Every one of the nine state protections for [off-duty cannabis use](#term:cannabis-testing-law) or against pre-employment THC testing excepts federal contracts, federal funding or [clearance](#term:security-clearance) work, so a protection that binds an ordinary employer stops at the [edge](#term:dependency-link) of a cleared position [219](#cite:219). Several state credit-check limits likewise except positions that require a security clearance, which the [FCRA](#term:fair-credit-reporting-act) gate records beside the federal notice duties that still apply [218](#cite:218). The federal gate sets the floor and the overlay adds duties or exceptions on top of it.

A change enacted but not yet in force is recorded apart from current law, so today's rule is not confused with next year's. The changes file dates each entry and gives it a status from a fixed vocabulary, proposed, announced, class-deviation, final, pending-implementation, suspended or withdrawn, and a superseded entry is marked, not deleted. Colorado is the clearest example. The 2024 AI Act never took effect: a stipulated order of April 27, 2026 barred its enforcement, and SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026, repealed and reenacted it as a notice-based law applying from January 1, 2027 [221](#cite:221) [222](#cite:222). The legislature's fiscal note describes the duties from that date, notice before [automated decision-making technology](#term:automated-employment-decision-tool) materially influences an employment decision, a description within 30 calendar days of an adverse outcome, meaningful human review, records kept at least three years, and Attorney General enforcement after a 60-day cure notice [222](#cite:222). The gate `ai-screening-laws` carries that as a pending change dated to 2027, and the entry that gave the old Act a 2026 effective date is marked superseded [222](#cite:222) [221](#cite:221). Washington is the other primary-sourced case. ESHB 1155 makes every noncompetition covenant void and unenforceable from June 30, 2027 regardless of when it was signed, sweeps repayment and forfeiture terms tied to working in one's field into the same category, keeps [nonsolicitation terms](#term:non-solicitation-agreement) with the customer restriction capped at 18 months, and requires notice to affected workers by October 1, 2027 [210](#cite:210). That one statute appears under the noncompete, stay-or-pay and [no-poach](#term:no-poach-agreement) gates and under the Washington state record [210](#cite:210).



The last thing to read in a gate is where its facts came from. The guide's standing rule is that law-firm, consultant and vendor commentary never carries a fact alone; it points at a primary source or flags a change, and where a gate rests on such a source its `conflicts` line says so and the primary fetch is logged as a todo. The gate `training-repayment-and-stay-or-pay` states that the California, New York, Connecticut, Colorado and Wyoming terms rest on law-firm summaries while Washington's rests on the statute [210](#cite:210). The state file makes the same admission: its header says the overlays rest on dated compilations, names the session laws and the fiscal note as the only primaries read in that sweep, and explains that `primary_pending: true` means no primary is among an overlay's sources, which the app renders as compilation-sourced, to be verified. A status of `none-found` means the state is absent from the named compilation as of its date, not that the state's law was checked.
picture: The state-overlay-counts figure is a row of nine horizontal bars, one per overlay. Each bar is divided by status in the overlay's own vocabulary, so the noncompete bar separates void, void-from-2027, income-threshold, category-limits and common-law. A hatched fill marks the segments whose records are compilation-sourced, and the few solid segments, the overlays with a primary behind them, stand out by their rarity. A caption under the cannabis bar notes that every statewide protection shown excepts federal contract and clearance work [219](#cite:219), so the bar reads as a map of where the overlay exists, not of where it reaches a cleared opening.

## How this guide uses it



Gates appear on every stage record, in the `gates` list naming the rules that bind that stage, with the clear-start stage carrying the most; on [constraint](#term:constraint-record) and [lever records](#term:lever-record) that name the rule the constraint runs into or the lever must respect; and in the [pathfinder](#term:pathfinder), whose state question selects the state record, after which the node panel for a gate lists the overlays that point at it. title: Reading an effect size
one_liner: What the coefficients on the guide's record cards mean, how to read a correlation, a d and an odds ratio, and how far a number from one firm travels.
why_here: Every lever in this guide carries an evidence grade and an effect size quoted as the study reported it, with its population; a recruiter without an HR department has to read those lines without a statistician and know when a figure is a direction and when it is a forecast.

further_reading.title: Revisiting meta-analytic estimates of validity in personnel selection: Addressing systematic overcorrection for restriction of range
Surveying the forest: A meta-analysis, moderator investigation, and future-oriented discussion of the antecedents of voluntary employee turnover
Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions decisions: A meta-analysis

body_before:
## What it is

The guide grades every [lever](#term:lever-record) by the design of the strongest study behind it. A [meta-analysis](#term:meta-analysis) grade means a published meta-analysis or systematic review, with the [effect size](#term:effect-size) quoted together with its [k and N](#term:k-and-n) as reported, which is the grade the 2022 selection table carries [1](#cite:1). [Field-experiment](#term:field-experiment) means a randomized or natural experiment in a real employment setting, as when employees were randomly told about a salary database [92](#cite:92); [quasi-experimental](#term:quasi-experimental-design) means a [difference-in-differences](#term:difference-in-differences), discontinuity or matched design on administrative data, as in the study of raises and quits at a large retailer [182](#cite:182); observational means survey research without a causal design, as in the one-firm study of [onboarding tactics](#term:socialization-tactics) [155](#cite:155); [practitioner-survey](#term:practitioner-survey) means a benchmark from a publisher such as SHRM or ClearanceJobs, carried as a dated fact and never as evidence of effect [89](#cite:89); regulation binds regardless of evidence; [synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker) is a conclusion no cited work states on its own, marked wherever a record makes one.

Most lines on the select and retain records are [correlations](#term:correlation-coefficient). A correlation coefficient, written r, or ρ when a meta-analysis has corrected it for measurement error and [range restriction](#term:range-restriction), runs from −1 to +1 and says how closely two measures move together. In the 2022 table, .42 for [structured interviews](#term:structured-interview) and .19 for unstructured ones means that interview scores track later performance much more closely when the interview is structured, and .07 for years of experience means a count of years tells almost nothing [1](#cite:1). The sign carries the direction: in the turnover table, [withdrawal cognitions](#term:withdrawal-cognitions) correlate .56 with leaving and [job embeddedness](#term:job-embeddedness) −.26, so wanting to leave goes with leaving and being embedded goes with staying [178](#cite:178).

A [standardized mean difference](#term:subgroup-difference), d, compares two groups' averages in units of the standard deviation. The 2022 table pairs each validity with a Black–White d so that the trade-off sits on one line: [cognitive ability](#term:cognitive-ability-test) pairs a validity of .31 with d = .79 and structured interviews .42 with .23, and the authors say the d values mix applicant, incumbent and national samples and are offered to locate predictors as having large, modest or minimal group differences [1](#cite:1).

Where the outcome is yes or no, such as leaving within a year, studies report [odds ratios](#term:odds-ratio). Below 1 means the factor goes with lower odds: in a one-firm study of 222 [newcomers](#term:newcomer-adjustment), experienced insiders as role models carried an OR of 0.44 for leaving within the year and affirmation of who the newcomer already is an OR of 0.52, which the author describes as roughly halving the odds [155](#cite:155). Above 1 means higher odds: among 157,154 accepted entry-level offers at one telecommunications employer, each additional week between acceptance and the start date carried an OR of 1.22 for the hire never appearing, about a fifth more per week as the authors put it, while an employee [referral](#term:referral-hiring) carried 0.42 [144](#cite:144).

k is the number of studies a meta-analysis pools and N the number of people across them; together they say how much of the world a figure has seen. The 2022 estimates rest on pooled databases such as k = 36 with N = 3,069 and k = 69 with N = 4,795 for structured interviews, and k = 54 with N = 10,469 for [work samples](#term:work-sample-test) [1](#cite:1); the turnover table on 316 articles, 57 predictors and about 1,800 effect sizes with a mean lag of about 16 months between predictor and leaving [178](#cite:178); the collective-turnover table on 694 effect sizes from 82 studies [181](#cite:181). The comparison of formula against judgment rests on nine job-performance studies, which is why its authors call the values probable underestimates [7](#cite:7). A meta-analysis is the top grade because it has seen many settings, and it still inherits its studies' populations: the turnover table is 78.9 percent U.S. samples, with healthcare at 25.9 percent and banking at 12.6 percent [178](#cite:178).

Several of the guide's most vivid numbers come from one employer and are carried for their shape. Output rose 53 percent over the first year for windshield installers at one autoglass company while pay rose much less; the job is manual, so the slope does not transfer and the shape does [157](#cite:157). The 24.8 percent first-year turnover figure is 222 newcomers at one financial-services firm with no standardized [orientation](#term:onboarding), so the direction is what carries [155](#cite:155). The guide names the population on every such line, and the controversy `cost-of-turnover` shows what happens when a number travels without one: practitioner literature repeats a total cost of 90 to 200 percent of salary that names no study [195](#cite:195), while the case-study median is 21 percent [180](#cite:180).

## The maths, gently

$$ r = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X, Y)}{s_X \, s_Y} \qquad d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{\text{pooled}}} \qquad \mathrm{OR} = \frac{p_1 / (1 - p_1)}{p_0 / (1 - p_0)} $$

- $r$: the correlation between a predictor $X$ (an interview score) and an outcome $Y$ (a performance rating); $\operatorname{cov}$ is their covariance and $s_X$ and $s_Y$ their standard deviations. A meta-analysis reports $\rho$, the same quantity corrected for unreliability and, where the authors judge it warranted, for range restriction [1](#cite:1).
- $d$: the difference between two group means, $\bar{x}_1$ and $\bar{x}_2$, divided by the pooled standard deviation $s_{\text{pooled}}$.
- $\mathrm{OR}$: the odds of the outcome when the factor is present, $p_1 / (1 - p_1)$, divided by the odds when it is absent, $p_0 / (1 - p_0)$; an odds ratio of 1 means no association.

Take the 2022 table [1](#cite:1). A structured interview at r = .42 and an unstructured one at .19 are both positive, so higher scores go with better performance under either method, and the structured coefficient is more than twice the size. Put d beside r: cognitive ability at .31 carries d = .79, the largest group difference in the table, while the structured interview at .42 carries .23, so the method with the higher validity also has the smaller difference [1](#cite:1).

## How this guide uses it

Every lever record carries a grade, an effect, a population and a k and N line in these terms: `l-structured-interview` carries the .42 and its two pooled databases [1](#cite:1), `l-embeddedness-building` carries ρ −.26 at k = 29 beside the one-firm OR of 0.42 [178](#cite:178) [155](#cite:155), and `l-offer-to-start-interval-management` carries the per-week OR of 1.22 with its entry-level population [144](#cite:144). Each [constraint](#term:constraint-record) names the strongest grade among its sources, the [indicator](#term:indicator-record) `ind-turnover-predictors-rubenstein2018` is the turnover table itself [178](#cite:178), and the methods page lists the grades, the [hypothesis ledger](#term:hypothesis-ledger) and every synthesis the records mark.

title: The clearance process, from sponsorship to access
one_liner: A contractor cannot start a clearance on its own schedule, cannot keep a bench of cleared people, and does not run the clock between an accepted offer and a badge.
why_here: At a customer-governed small firm the clearance clock is often longer than the opening can wait, and the rules that set it were written around the government's needs, not the firm's; a recruiter who knows the rules first can see which start dates are possible before promising one.

further_reading.title: 32 CFR § 117.10, Determination of eligibility for access to classified information (National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual rule)
Security Executive Agent Directive 7, Reciprocity of Background Investigations and National Security Adjudications
Personnel security clearances: Actions needed to address significant data reliability issues that impact oversight (GAO-26-107100)
Trusted Workforce 2.0 quarterly progress report, FY2026 Q3

body_before:
## What it is

A [security clearance](#term:security-clearance) for a contractor employee begins with a request the firm may make only in narrow circumstances. Under the [NISPOM rule](#term:nispom), eligibility is requested only where access is essential to a classified contract, for the minimum number of employees, and never to build a cache of cleared staff [119](#cite:119). A candidate can be investigated before employment, but only on a written commitment the candidate accepted in writing, and employment must then begin within 45 days of the grant [119](#cite:119). Where nothing adverse has surfaced the cognizant agency may grant [temporary eligibility](#term:temporary-eligibility), limited to one year without approval and valid at its level but not for RD, COMSEC or NATO information until the final grant; its withdrawal is not a denial and cannot be appealed [119](#cite:119). No public figure says how often a contractor applicant receives an interim or how long that decision takes [127](#cite:127).

Behind every personnel request stands a [facility clearance](#term:facility-clearance) the firm cannot obtain by asking. A contractor cannot apply for its own entity eligibility determination; a government contracting activity or a cleared contractor [sponsors](#term:clearance-sponsorship) it on a legitimate requirement, the firm's senior management official, facility security officer and insider-threat official must themselves hold eligibility, and foreign ownership, control or influence must not be disqualifying [120](#cite:120). [DCSA](#term:dcsa)'s roadmap puts the key officials' [questionnaires](#term:sf-86) and fingerprints at day 45 of the sponsorship and gives no [end-to-end](#term:end-to-end-timeliness) time [146](#cite:146). A clearance already held elsewhere is meant to travel: under SEAD 7 an agency accepts another authorized agency's investigation and adjudication unless one of seven exceptions applies, such as an investigation older than seven years or an interim grant, the determination is due within five business days, and [reciprocity](#term:reciprocity) cannot be withheld because a [polygraph](#term:polygraph) is wanted [122](#cite:122). GAO found the practice looser than the rule, with reciprocity data inconsistent and incomplete, 28 of 31 surveyed agencies saying their systems at times lacked the information a decision needs, and contractors reporting no status updates while a transfer was delayed [145](#cite:145).

The decision itself applies thirteen [adjudicative guidelines](#term:adjudicative-guidelines), from allegiance and foreign influence through financial considerations to the use of information technology, each with conditions that raise a concern and conditions that mitigate it, under the whole-person concept: "All available, reliable information about the person, past and present, favorable and unfavorable, should be considered" [123](#cite:123). The [Bond Amendment](#term:bond-amendment) sits above the weighing, since an unlawful drug user or addict is ineligible with no waiver [123](#cite:123). A favorable grant then opens a standing obligation. The contractor reports adverse information about cleared employees from verified sources, a duty that survives the employee's termination, along with suspicious contacts, terminations, citizenship changes and changes in its own key management personnel [189](#cite:189). The employee reports under SEAD 3: unofficial foreign travel at least five days before departure, continuing foreign contacts, debts over 120 days delinquent, arrests, treatment, cohabitants and conflicting outside employment, and a failure to report can affect eligibility [190](#cite:190). Industry accounted for roughly 984,000 [continuous-vetting](#term:continuous-vetting) enrollments in FY2026 Q3 [126](#cite:126), and full enrollment is planned for September 2028 [54](#cite:54).

The clocks are where the rule and the plan part company. [Trusted Workforce 2.0](#term:trusted-workforce-2) targets are 40 days end to end for a moderate-risk position and 75 for a high-risk one; the FY2026 Q3 report put DCSA's [investigation inventory](#term:investigation-inventory) at about 121,000 and rising, moved its reporting from the fastest 90 percent of cases to all cases, and said performance "remains much too high compared to performance targets" [54](#cite:54). DCSA's industry figures for that quarter averaged 197 days for a [Secret](#term:secret) (21 initiation, 59 investigation, 117 adjudication) and 243 for a [Top Secret](#term:top-secret) (20, 97, 126), with adjudication now the longest phase [126](#cite:126) [125](#cite:125); the last fastest-90-percent figures, for FY2026 Q1, were 156 and 227 days and cannot be compared with the new basis [124](#cite:124). GAO's caveat applies to all of them: 36 of 42 timeliness statistics it reviewed were inaccurate, mostly through a DCSA calculation error that understated clearance times from 2020 to 2024 [56](#cite:56). The guide records the disagreement as the controversy `clearance-timeliness-figures`. The wait has a measured cost of its own. Among 157,154 accepted entry-level offers at one telecommunications employer, 4.1 percent of hires never showed up, and each additional week between acceptance and the start date raised the odds of a [no-show](#term:new-hire-no-show) by about a fifth (OR 1.22), while a [referral](#term:referral-hiring) (OR 0.42) and good communication from the company (OR 0.56) lowered them [144](#cite:144). That population is entry-level and customer-facing, so the rate does not transfer to cleared technical hiring; the mechanism is what the guide carries [144](#cite:144).
picture: The clearance-clock figure is a horizontal timeline that starts at an accepted offer. Two stacked bars show DCSA's industry averages for FY2026 Q3, a Secret bar of 197 days divided into 21 days of initiation, 59 of investigation and 117 of adjudication, and a Top Secret bar of 243 days divided 20, 97 and 126 [126](#cite:126). Two short reference marks above the bars show the 40-day and 75-day targets [54](#cite:54), and a third mark at about 45 days shows the median [time to fill](#term:time-to-fill) a role [43](#cite:43). At the right-hand end of each bar a bracket of 45 days shows the period within which a pre-employment hire must start after the grant [119](#cite:119), and a footnote says the published statistics understated real processing time from 2020 to 2024 [56](#cite:56).

## How this guide uses it

The process is the spine of the `clear-start` stage and of the [failure pattern](#term:failure-pattern) `accept-cannot-start`, whose [constraints](#term:constraint-record) run in the order the evidence suggests: `c-sponsorship-needs-contract-and-fcl` [119](#cite:119) [120](#cite:120), `c-clearance-clock-exceeds-vacancy-window` [126](#cite:126) [43](#cite:43), `c-eligibility-is-not-access` [122](#cite:122) [145](#cite:145), `c-long-interval-loses-accepted-hires` [144](#cite:144) and `c-no-chargeable-work-before-access`, the unbillable payroll in the interval [148](#cite:148). The [gates](#term:gate-record) that carry the governing text are `nispom-eligibility-and-sponsorship`, `facility-clearance-sponsorship`, `temporary-eligibility`, `reciprocity-sead-7`, `adjudicative-guidelines-sead-4` and `nispom-reporting-and-continuous-vetting` [119](#cite:119) [120](#cite:120) [122](#cite:122) [123](#cite:123) [189](#cite:189).

title: The cost of a vacancy, in three parts
one_liner: An open requisition costs the firm what it spends to fill it, what the empty seat does to delivery and to the people covering it, and the cash it fronts between payroll and payment; only the first shows on an invoice.
why_here: At a customer-governed small firm the invoice stops when the seat is empty and payroll starts before the first invoice clears, so a recruiter who can price all three parts can rank openings by what each one costs.

## What it is



The guide's plan records treat what an opening costs as three separate numbers, and the step of putting them side by side is the guide's own. The first is [acquisition spend](#term:cost-per-hire), the one that appears in a budget line. SHRM's 2025 [benchmarking survey](#term:practitioner-survey) of 2,371 members put the median cost per hire at \$1,200 for nonexecutive roles, down 27 percent since 2017, and \$10,625 for executive roles, up 113 percent, with the figure defined as agency fees, job boards, [referral](#term:referral-hiring) costs, travel, relocation, recruiter pay and benefits, and systems, divided by hires [196](#cite:196). The clock that spend runs against is a median [time to fill](#term:time-to-fill) of about 45 days for executive and nonexecutive roles alike, with 41 percent of organizations citing rising [candidate ghosting](#term:candidate-ghosting) [43](#cite:43).

The second number is the vacancy itself. Across 27 case studies that excluded executives and physicians, the median [cost of replacing](#term:replacement-cost) a worker was about 21 percent of annual salary, 16 percent for jobs paying \$30,000 or less and up to 213 percent for very highly paid roles, and only 2 of the 11 papers reviewed counted [indirect costs](#term:overhead-rate) at all [180](#cite:180). At the level of the unit, a [meta-analysis](#term:meta-analysis) of 694 [effect sizes](#term:effect-size) from 82 studies found [turnover rates](#term:collective-turnover) correlated about −.22 with customer satisfaction and production efficiency, −.15 with profit margin and +.14 with error and loss rates, the same for voluntary and total turnover, while staffing levels and straight pay were not significantly related to turnover [181](#cite:181). In German administrative records of 34,000 unexpected worker deaths, the firm raised the wages and retention of the remaining workers in the same occupation, coworkers in other occupations lost when a high-skilled or specialized worker died, and replacement costs were substantial and larger in thin labor markets and for specialized skills [193](#cite:193). The people covering an empty seat carry a cost of their own that does not show as hours: stress and exhaustion predict quitting at ρ .21, role conflict and role ambiguity at .15 each and work–life conflict at .19, while hours of workload as such barely register at −.10 [178](#cite:178).

The third number is cash, and it comes from the contract and the payment rules. A [time-and-materials](#term:time-and-materials-contract) or labor-hour contract pays a fixed hourly rate for labor that meets a specified category's qualifications and is performed on the contract, and hours worked by employees who do not meet them are not paid without the contracting officer's authorization [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99). Labor that is not charged to a contract is an indirect cost, accumulated in pools and allocated across the firm's other work through its rates [148](#cite:148). Where the contract sets no date a [proper invoice](#term:prompt-payment) is due to be paid 30 days after the start of the payment period, an improper invoice is returned within 7 days and interest is paid automatically on late payments [202](#cite:202); agencies are directed to provide [accelerated payments](#term:accelerated-payment) to small business contractors with a goal of 15 days, and [primes](#term:prime-contractor) that receive them pass the acceleration to small [subcontractors](#term:subcontractor) within 15 days, although the goal creates no new Prompt Payment Act rights [201](#cite:201).

Two measurements sit at the [edges](#term:dependency-link), and one dispute runs through them. Where output could be counted per worker, among windshield installers at one U.S. autoglass company, output was 53 percent higher after one year than at hire, with pay profiles much flatter than output for the first 18 months; the work is manual, so the slope does not transfer to technical staff, only the shape [157](#cite:157). Before the [ramp](#term:time-to-productivity) can begin the hire has to arrive: among 157,154 accepted entry-level offers at one telecommunications employer, 4.1 percent never showed up, and each additional week between acceptance and start raised the odds of a [no-show](#term:new-hire-no-show) by about a fifth (OR 1.22) [144](#cite:144). The dispute is the multiple. A trade white paper puts direct [turnover costs](#term:cost-of-turnover) at 50 to 60 percent of salary and total costs at 90 to 200 percent and names no study for either figure [195](#cite:195), while the measured median across the case studies is 21 percent [180](#cite:180); the guide carries the disagreement as the controversy `cost-of-turnover`, with the unit-level [correlations](#term:correlation-coefficient) and the specialist case as the positions in between [181](#cite:181) [193](#cite:193).
picture: The cost-of-a-hire figure is three columns for one opening, drawn to different scales and labeled as such. The first column is acquisition spend, marked at the 2025 medians of \$1,200 and \$10,625 [196](#cite:196). The second is the vacancy, marked at the 21 percent case-study median with the 16 percent and 213 percent ends of the range as faint ticks [180](#cite:180) and annotated with the unit-level correlation of −.22 with customer satisfaction [181](#cite:181). The third is drawn as a timeline: payroll running from the start date, shaded as indirect cost until the first chargeable hour [148](#cite:148), then the 30-day default to payment with the 15-day goal marked inside it [202](#cite:202) [201](#cite:201). Above the second column a dashed ghost column rises to the 90 to 200 percent multiple, labeled as resting on no named study [195](#cite:195), and a thin line across the top traces output at 53 percent above the hire-date level after one year [157](#cite:157).

title: The labor category and the wrap rate
one_liner: On a time-and-materials contract each labor category has a fixed hourly rate that already contains the wage, the indirect costs and the profit, and it pays only for people who meet the category's qualifications.
why_here: The salary a customer-governed small firm can offer is what is left of a rate it agreed to at award; a recruiter who can read the category line and the layers between a salary and a billing rate knows before posting whether the market price of the person fits.

body_before:
## What it is

A [time-and-materials](#term:time-and-materials-contract) or labor-hour contract pays for work at fixed hourly rates set per [labor category](#term:labor-category), and FAR 16.601 defines the hourly rate as the contract rate for labor that meets the qualifications of a specified category [98](#cite:98). Those rates already include wages, [overhead](#term:overhead-rate), [general and administrative expense](#term:general-and-administrative-rate) and profit, and a ceiling price is required [98](#cite:98).

The qualifications become a hiring [constraint](#term:constraint-record) because the payment clause makes them one. Labor hours for tasks with specified qualifications are not paid to the extent the work is performed by employees who do not meet them, unless the contracting officer authorizes it, and each voucher must be supported by records showing those qualifications [99](#cite:99). The rule is enforced after the fact: an Inspector General audit of twelve OASIS task orders found DoD improperly charged for 101 of 112 employees who did not meet [labor-category requirements](#term:labor-category-qualifications), found that contracting officers had not validated 1,219 of 1,287 qualifications by résumé review, and put the potential improper payments at about \$35 million [173](#cite:173). A candidate who could do the work but misses the category's education or years line cannot be billed against it [99](#cite:99) [173](#cite:173).

Under cost-type contracts a second rule applies to the pay itself. Compensation is [allowable](#term:allowable-cost) when it is reasonable for the work and conforms to an established plan or consistent practice, with reasonableness judged against firms of similar size, industry and area doing similar non-government work; bonuses are allowable only under an agreement or plan established before the services; and compensation above the benchmark set under 41 U.S.C. 1127 is unallowable for all employees on awards from June 24, 2014 [100](#cite:100). The cap stood at \$671,000 for 2025 by an accounting firm's figure, with the OFPP determination itself still on the pack's to-do list [107](#cite:107).

Between a salary and a [billing rate](#term:wrap-rate) sit the layers a government cost proposal assumes, and the Department of Transportation's SBIR instructions state them plainly: fringe benefits are allocated on labor, overhead is applied to direct labor plus fringe, general and administrative expense is applied to total cost input, and profit is entered as a rate; rates approved by an agency such as [DCAA](#term:dcaa) within the past 30 months are used [206](#cite:206). The same layers are where unbillable payroll goes, since labor not charged to a contract is an indirect cost, pooled and allocated on a common base [148](#cite:148).



Put the two halves together and the salary ceiling appears. The category rate was fixed at award and moves only through the contract's adjustment mechanism, which on GSA schedules allows at most three increases a contract period inside a request window [117](#cite:117), while the market moves every month: private-industry wages rose 3.1 percent and benefits 3.8 percent in the year to June 2026 [103](#cite:103). Market pay for the occupation is public, software developers at a median of \$65.38 an hour in May 2025 [110](#cite:110), and awarded ceiling rates for comparable categories are public in CALC+ [111](#cite:111). Where the market salary loaded with the firm's fringe, overhead, G&A and profit exceeds the category rate, the role loses money at any hire, and the moves left are to redistribute the work, deliver it as a team at mixed categories, or change the rate or the scope, each of which the contract may bar [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99) [117](#cite:117) [206](#cite:206). No source states the test as such; the guide marks it as [synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker).
picture: A single vertical bar for one hour of one person's labor, read from the bottom up: the lowest segment is the direct wage; on it sits fringe; on wage and fringe together sits overhead; on everything below sits G&A; on top of it all sits profit, and the full height is the firm's loaded rate [206](#cite:206). Beside the bar a horizontal line marks the category's contract rate, fixed at award and movable only at the adjustment windows [98](#cite:98) [117](#cite:117). When the bar's top clears the line the category can be staffed at that wage; when it does not, the gap is the amount by which the loaded cost exceeds what the contract pays [98](#cite:98).

## The maths, gently

$$ R = S \times (1 + f) \times (1 + o) \times (1 + g) \times (1 + p) $$

- $R$: the loaded hourly rate the firm needs for one hour of this person's labor, compared with the category's contract rate or the schedule ceiling [98](#cite:98) [111](#cite:111).
- $S$: the direct hourly wage, the salary divided by the hours in the firm's labor base.
- $f$: the [fringe rate](#term:fringe-rate), applied to labor [206](#cite:206).
- $o$: the overhead rate, applied to labor plus fringe [206](#cite:206).
- $g$: the general and administrative rate, applied to total cost input, the whole stack below it [206](#cite:206).
- $p$: profit, entered as a rate on top [206](#cite:206).

The pack carries the first input and the last, the [OEWS](#term:oews) median of \$65.38 an hour for software developers in May 2025 [110](#cite:110) and the CALC+ ceiling rates [111](#cite:111). It carries no fringe, overhead, G&A or [profit rate](#term:fee) for any firm, because those are the firm's own, taken from its approved rates or the calculations behind them [206](#cite:206), so no worked figure is given here; the [lever](#term:lever-record) `l-wrap-rate-feasibility-check` states the same multiplication [206](#cite:206).

## How this guide uses it

The [gate](#term:gate-record) `tm-labor-category-rates` carries FAR 16.601 and 52.232-7 [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99); `far-31-205-6-compensation-allowability` carries the cost principle and the cap, which is also the [indicator](#term:indicator-record) `ind-contractor-comp-cap-2025` [100](#cite:100) [107](#cite:107); `contract-price-adjustment-limits` carries the adjustment mechanics [117](#cite:117). The arithmetic drives the offer-stage constraint `c-salary-above-rate`, the plan-stage constraint `c-role-structurally-unprofitable` and the levers `l-set-range-from-rate-and-market`, `l-wrap-rate-feasibility-check` and `l-rate-relief-request` [98](#cite:98) [206](#cite:206) [103](#cite:103).

The qualification rule drives `c-customer-rejects-junior-staff` and `c-firm-and-customer-define-qualified-differently`, with the audit as their indicator `ind-oasis-improper-payments-2018` and `l-supervised-junior-work-package` as the lever that bills each person at the category they meet [99](#cite:99) [173](#cite:173). Payroll during a [clearance](#term:security-clearance) wait sits in the same indirect pools, which is `c-no-chargeable-work-before-access` [148](#cite:148), and the [enabler](#term:enabler-record) `dot-sbir-cost-proposal-instructions` points at the build-up itself [206](#cite:206).

title: What predicts a good hire
one_liner: Scored evidence of the work itself, a structured interview, a knowledge test or a work sample, predicts job performance; an unscored conversation and a count of years on a résumé barely do.
why_here: The recruiter at a customer-governed small firm chooses the method, and the method decides who gets hired, how large the group differences in selection rates will be, and what the firm can show a customer or an agency about why it chose as it did.

## What it is

The question of which hiring methods predict later job performance has a current standard answer, the 2022 re-estimation by Sackett, Zhang, Berry and Lievens, which took the databases behind the earlier [meta-analyses](#term:meta-analysis) and recalculated each method's [operational validity](#term:operational-validity), the [correlation](#term:correlation-coefficient) between a score at hiring and performance on the job [1](#cite:1). The revised table puts [structured interviews](#term:structured-interview) first at .42, then [job-knowledge tests](#term:job-knowledge-test) at .40, [empirically keyed biodata](#term:biodata) at .38, [work samples](#term:work-sample-test) at .33, and [cognitive ability](#term:cognitive-ability-test) and [integrity tests](#term:integrity-test) at .31 each; [unstructured interviews](#term:unstructured-interview) sit at .19 and years of job experience at .07 [1](#cite:1). Read as a ranking, the table says that a scored conversation about the work, a test of what the job requires, or a sample of the work itself tells a firm far more than an unscored conversation or a count of years on a résumé [1](#cite:1).

These figures are lower than the ones selection textbooks carried for two decades. Schmidt and Hunter's 1998 summary of 85 years of research put general mental ability at .51, the structured interview at .51, work samples at .54 and the unstructured interview at .38 [4](#cite:4). The 2022 authors showed that the earlier work had applied [range-restriction corrections](#term:range-restriction) derived from [predictive studies](#term:validation-study), where applicants are tested and then hired before their performance is known, to the concurrent studies of people already on the job that dominate the databases, and that this overcorrected; without that correction the estimates fall by .10 to .20, the rank order of the strong predictors largely holds, and cognitive ability moves well down the list [1](#cite:1). Whether concurrent studies need no correction at all is disputed in print [2](#cite:2), and the guide carries the dispute as the controversy `cognitive-ability-validity`; the ordering that matters to a small firm, structure above judgment, is common to both sides [1](#cite:1) [4](#cite:4).

Each validity in the revised table is paired with a Black–White [standardized difference](#term:subgroup-difference), d, so that the cost of a predictor is visible beside its benefit: cognitive ability carries d = .79, work samples .67, job-knowledge tests .54, [assessment centers](#term:assessment-center) .52, years of experience .49, unstructured interviews .32, structured interviews .23 and integrity tests .10 [1](#cite:1). The cognitively loaded measures with the most validity show the largest group differences, and the structured interview is the method that pairs high validity with a modest one, with a caveat the guide keeps beside it: two behavioral interviews used as a first screen showed d of .36 and .56 once range restriction was corrected [18](#cite:18). The authors say the d values mix applicant, incumbent and national samples and are offered to locate predictors as having large, modest or minimal group differences [1](#cite:1).

How the evidence is combined matters as much as which evidence is collected. When the same predictor information is combined by formula instead of by judgment, prediction of job performance rises from r = .28 to .44 across nine comparisons, and the authors conclude that experts collect information well and combine it poorly [7](#cite:7). Field evidence from fifteen service-sector firms that introduced a pre-employment test points the same way: managers who hired against the test's recommendation made worse hires on average, and the test scores better identified the workers who would stay [10](#cite:10). Applicants have a ranking of their own. Across 86 samples and 48,750 people, interviews (3.84 on a five-point scale) and work samples (3.63) were the best-liked procedures, honesty tests (2.47) and graphology (1.76) the least liked, and those perceptions predict attraction to the employer, intention to accept an offer and willingness to recommend it [14](#cite:14).
picture: A scatter plot with operational validity on the horizontal axis and the Black–White d on the vertical, one labeled point per method from the 2022 table: structured interviews sit far to the right and low (.42, .23), cognitive ability to the right of center and high (.31, .79), work samples between them (.33, .67), and unstructured interviews and years of experience near the left [edge](#term:dependency-link) (.19 and .07) [1](#cite:1). The methods that are both predictive and modest in group difference gather in the lower right, where the guide's select-stage [levers](#term:lever-record) sit; a dotted second marker for the structured interview at d = .36 and .56 keeps the first-screen caveat on the page [18](#cite:18).

## How this guide uses it

The [Uniform Guidelines](#term:uniform-guidelines) are the frame the figures sit in. An employer keeps selection rates by sex and by race or ethnic group, and a group's rate below [four-fifths](#term:four-fifths-rule) of the highest group's is generally regarded as evidence of [adverse impact](#term:adverse-impact), qualified by statistical and practical significance and by small numbers [31](#cite:31); a procedure with adverse impact needs criterion-related, content or construct validity evidence tied to important elements of job performance, with cutoffs set to normal expectations of proficiency and more evidence for ranking than for pass/fail use [32](#cite:32); the eighteen sections were adopted jointly by the EEOC, the Civil Service Commission, DOL and DOJ in 1978 [30](#cite:30). The [gate](#term:gate-record) `ugesp` carries these rules and `eeoc-selection-procedures` the EEOC's plain map of them, including the employer's continuing responsibility for a vendor's test [33](#cite:33).

In the records, the table is the evidence behind the select-stage [constraints](#term:constraint-record) `c-unstructured-judgement`, `c-keyword-screen-rejects-qualified`, where years of experience at .07 is the proxy a keyword screen encodes, and `c-validity-diversity-tradeoff`, and behind the levers `l-structured-interview`, `l-work-sample-or-knowledge-test` and `l-mechanical-scoring`, whose effect lines carry the .42, the .40 and .33, and the .44 against .28 [1](#cite:1) [7](#cite:7). title: Who pays for training
one_liner: Theory says the worker pays for skills any employer can use; in practice the firm pays, keeps part of the return while the person stays, and finds the law narrowing the ways it can hold the investment.
why_here: A small technical firm trains people in portable skills, often out of its seniors' billable hours; a recruiter who knows why the firm trains at all, and what it may lawfully ask in return, can write a development offer that attracts and keeps people without a clause that is unlawful in the strictest states.

body_before:
## What it is

Economists divide what a worker learns into [general human capital](#term:general-human-capital), skills any employer can use, and [specific human capital](#term:specific-human-capital), skills worth something only at the firm that taught them. The standard theory, as Acemoglu and Pischke restate it, says workers pay for general training because they can take it anywhere, so a firm should fund only firm-specific skills [161](#cite:161). Their 1998 paper offers a theory in which workers do not pay for the general training they receive: the current employer knows the trained worker's ability better than rival employers do, that information advantage gives it ex post monopsony power, and the power makes paying for general skills worthwhile; German [apprentice](#term:registered-apprenticeship) data give the predictions some support [161](#cite:161). For a small firm the point is that it trains because it knows what the trained person can do [161](#cite:161).

The return arrives as a wedge between what the trained person produces and what they are paid. On a panel of British industries from 1983 to 1996, a one percentage point increase in training was associated with an increase of about 0.6 percent in value added per hour and about 0.3 percent in hourly wages, so output rose about twice as much as pay and the firm kept the difference while the person stayed [159](#cite:159). Part of what a firm spends is not a course at all. On German establishment data, workers with higher-paid coworkers had faster wage growth, and between 4 and 9 percent of total compensation took the form of learning from more knowledgeable coworkers [158](#cite:158); for a firm with one senior per specialty that is what [mentoring](#term:mentoring) costs in billable hours, which is the [constraint](#term:constraint-record) `c-mentoring-capacity-is-senior-billable-time` [158](#cite:158) [99](#cite:99).

Paying for education keeps people, but mostly by changing who applies. At one large establishment that adopted a tuition-reimbursement program, retention rose, and 80 percent of the program's overall effect came through sorting, who chose to join the firm, with the remainder through participation [160](#cite:160). Whether a course changes anything on the job is a separate question. The transfer-of-training review finds the most consistent support for realistic training environments, behavioral modeling and error management in the design, a supervisor who expects the skill to be used (ρ .31, against .14 for peer support), a [transfer climate](#term:transfer-of-training) (.37) and an early opportunity to perform, with motivation to transfer at .43 against .07 for motivation to learn; the often-repeated estimate that only 10 percent of training spending transfers is a 1982 figure, not a measurement [162](#cite:162).

The instruments a firm once used to hold the investment are narrowing. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau treats [training repayment provisions](#term:training-repayment-agreement) as employer-driven debt: nearly 10 percent of American workers surveyed in 2020 were covered by one, 44.8 percent of nurses with five years or less, with repayment demands documented far above the training's cost, and the research the Bureau cites puts a training contract's effect at around 15 percent less quitting [166](#cite:166).

California's AB 692 makes it unlawful, for contracts entered after January 1, 2026, to require repayment of training, education, relocation, signing or retention amounts for leaving before a date, with exceptions for a transferable credential under a separate, prorated, at-cost agreement and for [signing bonuses](#term:signing-bonus) on stated conditions, no repayment on a termination except for misconduct, and a \$5,000 penalty or actual damages [167](#cite:167). Colorado permits repayment only for training distinct from normal on-the-job training, at reasonable cost declining proportionally over two years, and Connecticut bars [promissory notes](#term:employment-promissory-note) as a condition of employment [168](#cite:168). New York's Trapped at Work Act, signed December 19, 2025 and amended February 13, 2026, makes employment promissory notes unenforceable from February 13, 2027, with exceptions for bonuses and tuition toward a transferable credential, and fines of \$1,000 to \$5,000 per violation [212](#cite:212) [211](#cite:211). Washington's [noncompete](#term:noncompete-agreement) statute, effective June 30, 2027, treats repayment and forfeiture terms tied to working in one's field as void noncompetes and leaves outside the ban a written agreement to repay out-of-pocket educational expenses that expires within 18 months of the start date [210](#cite:210). The federal positions moved the other way: the NLRB general counsel's memoranda against [stay-or-pay terms](#term:stay-or-pay-provision) were rescinded and the FTC rule that would have treated some provisions as noncompetes is not in effect [168](#cite:168).

On the cost side the rules are permissive. Training and education related to the field in which the employee works or may reasonably be expected to work are [allowable costs](#term:allowable-cost), except overtime for training, salaries for attending undergraduate or part-time graduate classes in working hours absent unusual circumstances, full-time graduate education beyond two school years, and training for other than bona fide employees [175](#cite:175). Up to \$5,250 per employee per year of [educational assistance](#term:section-127-plan) is excludable from wages under a separate written plan with notice to employees, covering tuition, fees, books and, since March 27, 2020 and now without an end date, principal and interest on the employee's own education loans; the amount is indexed for taxable years after 2026 [174](#cite:174).



The guide holds these findings together in the controversy `who-pays-for-training`, with five positions: the standard theory, the information-advantage account, the productivity–wage wedge, the sorting result, and the regulators' view that repayment provisions shift cost and risk to the worker and chill mobility whether or not enforced [161](#cite:161) [159](#cite:159) [160](#cite:160) [166](#cite:166) [167](#cite:167) [168](#cite:168). Its reading, marked as [synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker), is that the return comes through the wedge while the person stays and through the applicants the offer attracts, not through a repayment clause [159](#cite:159) [160](#cite:160) [166](#cite:166).

## How this guide uses it

The develop stage carries the economics in the constraints `c-training-investment-walks-out`, `c-mentoring-capacity-is-senior-billable-time`, `c-training-content-unlike-the-work` and `c-development-return-unmeasured` [161](#cite:161) [158](#cite:158) [162](#cite:162) [159](#cite:159), and in the [levers](#term:lever-record) `l-training-with-lawful-retention-terms`, `l-protected-mentoring-time`, `l-representative-task-training` and `l-cohort-return-tracking` [160](#cite:160) [166](#cite:166) [162](#cite:162) [159](#cite:159). The [gates](#term:gate-record) are `training-repayment-and-stay-or-pay`, with the California, New York and Washington dates among its pending changes [167](#cite:167) [212](#cite:212) [210](#cite:210), `far-31-205-44-training-costs` [175](#cite:175), `section-127-educational-assistance` with the [indicator](#term:indicator-record) `ind-section-127-limit` [174](#cite:174), and `noncompete-agreements-federal-status` [169](#cite:169). The retain-stage constraint `c-poaching-by-prime-or-customer` is where the portable investment meets a larger employer's premium [161](#cite:161).

title: Why people leave
one_liner: Wanting to leave and looking are the strongest signals, then commitment, fit, satisfaction, embeddedness and the supervisor; pay is modest and works through comparison; hours as such barely register, strain does.
why_here: At a customer-governed small firm the person works under the customer's manager, at the customer's site, on a rate the firm cannot move freely; the ranked predictors tell a recruiter or hiring lead which of the things the firm still controls deserve its attention.

## What it is

The current map of why people quit is a [meta-analysis](#term:meta-analysis) of 316 articles and 57 predictors, about 1,800 [effect sizes](#term:effect-size) with a mean lag of about 16 months between the predictor and the leaving [178](#cite:178). Its ranking, as [corrected correlations](#term:correlation-coefficient) with voluntary turnover, runs: [withdrawal cognitions](#term:withdrawal-cognitions), wanting to leave, .56; job search .40; organizational commitment −.29; person–job and person–organization fit −.29; job satisfaction −.28; [job embeddedness](#term:job-embeddedness) −.26; leadership −.24; climate −.24; perceived alternatives .23; stress and exhaustion .21; age −.21; tenure −.20; work–life conflict .19; pay −.17; role ambiguity and role conflict .15 each; coworker support −.14; workload −.10; performance −.08, or −.21 with an outlier removed [178](#cite:178). Two moderators matter to a small firm: age and satisfaction matter more where base rates of leaving are higher, and alternatives matter more where withdrawal cognitions are high [178](#cite:178). The samples are 78.9 percent U.S., with healthcare at 25.9 percent and banking at 12.6 percent, so the ordering is what carries [178](#cite:178).

Embeddedness is the web of links, fit and sacrifice, on and off the job, that makes leaving costly. The plain-language summary the guide carries calls it moderately predictive of turnover and minimally predictive of performance, finds on-the-job embeddedness more predictive than off-the-job, and says the practices suggested to build it, teams, gatherings, fit and flexible scheduling, are untested [192](#cite:192). In a one-firm study of 222 [newcomers](#term:newcomer-adjustment), on-the-job embeddedness carried an [odds ratio](#term:odds-ratio) of 0.42 for leaving within the year and partly mediated the effect of [investiture](#term:socialization-tactics), the tactic that affirms who the newcomer already is [155](#cite:155). The [levers](#term:lever-record) the guide builds on this are `l-embeddedness-building`, which gives a person at a customer site a firm-side team, a [mentor](#term:mentoring) and a role in something the firm owns, and `l-manager-check-ins-and-stay-conversations`, which listens for the two strongest signals [178](#cite:178) [192](#cite:192).

Pay sits at −.17, below the supervisor and the alternatives, and the causal evidence says it moves people through comparison [178](#cite:178). At a large U.S. retailer, in a regression-discontinuity design on arbitrary differences in own and peer wages, the quit response to own pay mostly reflected comparisons with higher-paid peers, and separations were fairly insensitive when raises were similar across peers [182](#cite:182). When University of California employees were randomly informed of a public salary database, those paid below their unit's median reported lower satisfaction and were significantly more likely to look for a new job, and those above gained nothing [92](#cite:92). External hires into comparable jobs started about 18 percent higher than workers promoted into them at one financial-services firm [93](#cite:93).



Each market-rate hire therefore resets the incumbents' comparison point, which is the [constraint](#term:constraint-record) `c-new-hire-pay-compresses-incumbents` and the reason the lever `l-pay-review-against-market-and-peers` keeps raises similar across peers unless the difference can be explained [93](#cite:93) [182](#cite:182) [92](#cite:92).

The workload row is the one a firm covering a vacancy should read twice. Hours of workload as such correlate −.10 with leaving, while stress and exhaustion run .21, work–life conflict .19 and role ambiguity and role conflict .15 each [178](#cite:178); at the unit level, staffing levels were not significantly related to [turnover rates](#term:collective-turnover) [181](#cite:181).



The constraint `c-vacancy-overload-cascade` reads this to mean that covering a vacancy with the people who remain shows up as strain, conflict between roles and a lost boundary with home, not as hours on a utilization report, and `l-capacity-signalling-and-scope-negotiation` is the lever it carries [178](#cite:178) [181](#cite:181).

What turnover does to a unit, and what holds a unit together, is a second meta-analysis of 694 effect sizes from 82 studies [181](#cite:181). Turnover rates correlate about −.22 with customer satisfaction and production efficiency, −.15 with profit margin and +.14 with error and loss rates, the same for voluntary and total turnover; among the practices, [firm-specific training](#term:specific-human-capital) (−.40), internal mobility (−.25), staffing selectivity (−.24) and high-commitment HR systems (−.23) go with lower turnover, while straight pay, variable pay, staffing levels and [general training](#term:general-human-capital) were not significant [181](#cite:181). The cost of one departure is disputed. Across 27 case studies excluding executives and physicians, the median [replacement cost](#term:replacement-cost) was about 21 percent of annual salary, 16 percent for jobs paying \$30,000 or less and up to 213 percent for very highly paid roles, with only 2 of 11 papers counting [indirect costs](#term:overhead-rate) [180](#cite:180); the practitioner literature's total cost of 90 to 200 percent of salary names no study [195](#cite:195). The controversy `cost-of-turnover` holds both, with a natural experiment on worker deaths as a third position: replacement costs are substantial and largest for specialized skills and in thin labor markets, where the firm also pays the remaining specialists more [193](#cite:193).
picture: A horizontal bar chart of the turnover predictors from the meta-analysis, ordered by the size of the corrected correlation and signed: withdrawal cognitions (.56) and job search (.40) at the top, then the cluster of commitment, fit and satisfaction near −.3, embeddedness (−.26), leadership (−.24) and alternatives (.23), down through stress (.21), work–life conflict (.19) and pay (−.17) to workload (−.10) at the bottom [178](#cite:178). Shaded bands mark the three groups the records use, the signals, the attachments and the pressures, and a note beside the pay bar points to the comparison evidence, since the bar's length says how much pay predicts and not how it works [182](#cite:182).

## How this guide uses it

The retain stage's description is this ranking, and its [failure pattern](#term:failure-pattern) `productive-employees-leave` orders the constraints by it: `c-disconnection-from-the-firm-and-the-work` for commitment, fit, satisfaction, embeddedness and the supervisor; `c-pay-lags-capability-and-peers`; `c-few-steps-up-in-a-small-firm`, where internal mobility at −.25 meets the promotion evidence that a doubling of a manager's pre-promotion sales goes with a 7.5 percent decline in manager value added; `c-vacancy-overload-cascade`; `c-onsite-schedule-and-commute`; `c-contract-discontinuity-fear`, a visible contract end read as a withdrawal cognition; and `c-poaching-by-prime-or-customer` [178](#cite:178) [181](#cite:181) [185](#cite:185). The [indicators](#term:indicator-record) `ind-turnover-predictors-rubenstein2018`, `ind-collective-turnover-performance-2013` and `ind-turnover-cost-share-of-salary` carry the three tables with their populations and dates [178](#cite:178) [181](#cite:181) [180](#cite:180), and the plan-stage lever `l-vacancy-cost-estimate` takes the measured fifth of salary and the unit-level −.22 as its terms [180](#cite:180) [181](#cite:181).
